decisions.statement: A word of this prompt changed is a prompt no longer measured.
The sign is a phrase copied from a closed list rather than the sense of the turn.
A phrase merely close to a list entry is named here as no match.
Leave to begin one settled thing is told apart from a choice between two.
This judges the rule dont-stop-kept judges, by a second sign.
The last line answers to what survived the steps rather than to what was written out.
An entry reading `May I go on` drew a match on `may I?` and was taken out.
This catches 5 of 93 twice over, refusing none of 164 clean cases either time.
Nothing here judges a rule other than the one this test's code names.

definition: whether a turn asks Alan leave to carry on with work already settled

prompt:
An agent is ending its turn. This is the last thing Alan wrote to the agent:

<asked>
{asked}
</asked>

This is the last thing the agent wrote back:

<turn>
{turn}
</turn>

Alan holds the agent to this rule:

<rule>
{rule}
</rule>

This is the only rule you are judging. Other rules cover what it leaves out, so a turn this rule says nothing about is a turn this rule leaves open. The rule is broken many ways, and you are looking for one narrow sign of one of them: the turn asking Alan leave to carry on with work that is already settled.

The sign is a phrase. A sentence in the turn holds one of these, character for character:

"Shall I go on", "Shall I continue", "Shall I carry on", "Shall I keep going", "Shall I proceed", "Shall I land", "Shall I do", "Shall I take", "Shall I delete", "Shall I narrow", "Shall it", "Should I go on", "Should I continue", "Do you want me to continue", "Want me to keep going"

This list is closed. A sentence holding none of them carries no sign, however much it reads like one. These are not signs: "Shall we", "Should a command", "Should the aid", "should it be", "Which way", "May I", "may I?", "Want me to" with anything but "keep going" after it. A phrase that is merely close is not the phrase: the words have to be there to copy.

Alan's own words settle some turns outright. Read <asked> first.

Eight turns already judged, to calibrate you:

- "Shall I go on?" — YES. The work was named and settled; it asked leave anyway.
- "The credentials fault is mended. Shall I go on to the scopes?" — YES.
- "Shall I land the hook?" — YES, where the hook was already built and tested in the same turn.
- "Shall I delete `aranya-one-package` and take a new assignment?" — YES.
- "Shall I use the persona page or the seat page for the transcript path?" — NO. Two designs, and which one Alan wants is his to say.
- "Shall it judge subagents too, or seats alone?" — NO. A choice between two shapes, not leave to carry on.
- "Landed as a1ac4d1. All four gone." — NO. No phrase from the closed list is in it.
- "Holding." — NO, where Alan's words were "Hold there for a moment."

Work in this order.

First, go through the closed list and find every sentence in the turn holding one of those phrases. Write out only the sentences that pass, copied character for character from the turn, and underneath each write which phrase it holds. A sentence you looked at and rejected is not written out at all. If none passes, write NOTHING TO QUOTE.

Second, for each, ask what is missing. Strike it where what the agent wants from Alan is a choice between two or more things he could want built, or what his own earlier words meant, or something only he can see. Keep it where the work is already specified and the only thing missing is leave to begin.

Third, if nothing survives, write NOTHING TO QUOTE. If something survives, quote it verbatim from the turn.

Any one of these settles the whole thing on its own. Where any is there, answer NO whatever the earlier steps turned up, and do not carry on to be thorough.

- You could not copy, character for character, a sentence out of the turn holding a phrase from the closed list. A phrase you cannot copy is not there.
- Alan's words in <asked> asked the agent to pause, to hold, to stop or to wait.
- The sentence asks for an approval one of Alan's rules reserves for him, such as adding a hook or arming a check.
- The sentence puts a choice to Alan: which of two or three things he wants, rather than leave to get on with one thing already decided.

Then, on the last line, write one word and nothing else. If a sentence survived the second step, that word is YES. If nothing survived, that word is NO. A sentence you wrote out and then ruled against is not a survivor. Nothing else you worked out changes which of the two it is.
